agents.orchestration: Three parallel workflows of two topics each. Per topic: one research agent proposing claims with sources, quotes of at most 50 words, locators, archive captures, language and dated precision; for every proposed claim, two independent verifier agents in batches of five, each told to refute (one with a source-text lens, one with a proposition lens) and each retrieving the sources itself; a third adjudicating agent for every claim the two did not both uphold, deciding keep, keep with corrections, drop or move to stops on the source text; a completeness critic; and one extra round of research and verification for the gaps it found.
agents.independence: Verifiers received the proposed claims and source references but not each other’s verdicts; the adjudicator received both reports. Execution independence is not established.

missing.item: Anthropic's Frontier Compliance Framework documents themselves, in three editions: 'December 2025', 'March 2026', and 'Version 2, Effective 24th July 2026'. Each edition carries the explicit designation sentence. The December 2025 text reads: 'In the United States, the FCF serves as our Frontier AI Framework under California's Transparency in Frontier AI Act (TFAIA), documenting Anthropic PBC's technical and organizational protocols to manage, assess, and mitigate catastrophic risks.' The documents also refer to critical safety incidents 'in pursuant to Section 22757.13' of the TFAIA. The March 2026 edition adds a scope sentence tied to the TFAIA 'catastrophic risk' definition, a changelog, and a 12-month Framework Assessment 'from the Effective Dates of the TFAIA and the EU Code'.
missing.why: Both surviving Anthropic records (sb-anthropic-fcf-published, sb-link-anthropic-fcf) rest only on the 2025-12-19 announcement, which is forward-looking ('will serve'). The closest source is the instrument itself. It names the legal entity (Anthropic PBC), which parallels the OpenAI OpCo LLC record. The three editions and the changelog give dated edition records for the framework family, which matters for the annual-review and 30-day modification provisions. Record these as company statements only. Whether they satisfy § 22757.12 stays a stop. The 'December 2025' edition label is not a publication date. The live trust.anthropic.com page is a JavaScript shell (Vanta) that previously failed to retrieve. I retrieved all three PDFs from Internet Archive captures and extracted text with pdftotext: December 2025 is 4,233 words, March 2026 is 4,353 and Version 2 is 4,711.

missing.item: Definitions of 'critical safety incident' (§ 22757.11(d)) and 'deploy' (§ 22757.11(e)) in Bus. & Prof. Code. The critical safety incident definition has four limbs: (1) unauthorised access to, modification of, or exfiltration of frontier-model weights that results in death or bodily injury; (2) harm from the materialisation of a catastrophic risk; (3) loss of control of a frontier model causing death or bodily injury; (4) deceptive techniques against the developer to subvert its controls or monitoring, outside an evaluation, in a manner demonstrating materially increased catastrophic risk. 'Deploy' excludes making a model available to a third party for the primary purpose of developing or evaluating it.
missing.why: The incident-reporting claims (sb-critical-incident-15-days, sb-critical-incident-24-hours, sb-federal-equivalence-pathway) and the transparency-report trigger (sb-transparency-report) cannot be read without these definitions. Their thresholds and exclusions are the operative scope. The text is already in the chaptered bill the researcher extracted, at sb53_body.txt lines 48–57. The chaptered-text quote budget is nearly spent (372 of 400 words), so record these as labelled paraphrases.

missing.item: Lab. Code § 1107 contains a separate set of whistleblower definitions, plus remaining § 1107.1 duties. 'Covered employee' (§ 1107(b)) means an employee responsible for assessing, managing or addressing the risk of critical safety incidents. The § 1107 definitions of 'catastrophic risk' and 'critical safety incident' are keyed to 'foundation model', not 'frontier model'. In § 1107(c)(1), the weights limb also covers 'damage to, or loss of, property'. Lab. Code § 1107.2 adds that loss of equity value is not property damage. The remaining § 1107.1 duties are: a notice to covered employees of their rights, posted at all times or given in writing annually and acknowledged (§ 1107.1(d)); no contract may block disclosures protected by § 1102.5 (§ 1107.1(b)); attorney's fees; a burden shift to clear and convincing evidence once the employee shows a contributing factor; temporary injunctive relief not stayed pending appeal (§ 1107.1(f)–(i)).
missing.why: The surviving whistleblower records quote 'covered employee' and 'catastrophic risk' without the Labor Code definitions that govern them. They therefore implicitly import the Bus. & Prof. Code definitions, which differ textually: foundation model rather than frontier model, and the property limb. A researcher would treat the whistleblower scope as materially different. Record the textual difference only. What it means legally is a stop.

missing.item: Legislative history of SB 53, from introduction to enactment. Introduced 2025-01-07 by Senator Wiener. According to the author's 2025-07-09 release and the committee analyses, the introduced bill covered only CalCompute and whistleblower protection. Author's amendments of 2025-07-08 turned it into a transparency measure. Floor votes: Senate 2025-05-28 (Ayes 37, Noes 0); Assembly 2025-09-12 (Ayes 59, Noes 7); Senate concurrence 2025-09-13 (Ayes 29, Noes 8). The Assembly Privacy and Consumer Protection Committee analysis of the bill as amended 2025-09-05 (hearing 2025-09-11) lists what those amendments changed: the maximum civil penalty fell from $10 million to $1 million; the $500 million large-developer tier was added; the Attorney General's power to adjust scoping definitions by regulation was replaced with annual Department of Technology recommendations; contractors were removed from whistleblower protection; local preemption was added; internal-use assessments moved from public disclosure to confidential summaries for OES.
missing.why: The dataset has enactment and effective dates but nothing on how the enacted thresholds and penalty came about. Bill versions and official committee analyses are the closest sources for dated, version-specific claims, such as that the $1M cap replaced an earlier $10M figure. Without them, the record cannot separate the enacted text from earlier versions. The vote counts are in hist.txt, which the researcher already retrieved. I retrieved the committee analysis (13,102 words, pdftotext). Note that it misnames OES as the 'Office of Emergency Management'. Record bill version, actions and votes. Do not attribute motives to any person.

stops.issue: METR's 'Frontier AI safety regulations: A reference for lab staff' (2026-01-29) states that developers such as OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and xAI are governed by SB 53 obligations. Whether the statute applies to a named company is legal application and is not recorded. No record states that any company is a frontier developer or large frontier developer.

The Midas Project has alleged that OpenAI violated SB 53: over GPT-5.3-Codex (reported February 2026) and over later system cards (reported September 2026). OpenAI disputes this, partly by contesting how its Preparedness Framework wording should be read. Whether a developer violated or complied with SB 53, and how framework wording is construed for SB 53 purposes, are legal determinations. Not recorded. Seen only in search-result summaries; the articles were not retrieved or inspected.

Company designations recorded as statements only, never as legal fact: OpenAI's statement that OpenAI OpCo LLC is responsible for TFAIA compliance; xAI's statement that its December 2025 FAIF 'complies' with TFAIA; Anthropic's designation of the FCF (not the RSP) as its SB 53 compliance framework. Whether any of these satisfies § 22757.12, and whether those entities are the legally responsible developers, needs interpretation.

Federal preemption and federal-contract carve-outs: SB 53 SEC. 5(d) (no application to the extent of strict conflict with a federal government contract), SEC. 5(e) (no application to the extent preempted by federal law) and SEC. 5(f) (preemption of local rules adopted on or after 2025-01-01). Whether any federal law or action preempts or limits SB 53 is legal interpretation and was not examined.

What 'comply with' one's own framework (§ 22757.12(a); penalty ground in § 22757.15(a)) means when a framework uses discretionary or hedged language, and what counts as a 'material modification' (§ 22757.12(b)(2)) or a 'substantially modified' model (§ 22757.12(c)), are questions of statutory interpretation. Not resolved.
